question: Do denoising diffusion models learn low-order distribution statistics before higher-order correlations, and what data, architecture, and optimization quantities determine the sample complexity of that progression?

key_findings.claim: A grayscale CIFAR-10 U-Net initially behaves as if the data were Gaussian with matching mean and covariance, then becomes sensitive to higher-order image statistics after roughly one thousand optimization steps.
key_findings.evidence: For about the first 10^3 steps, test denoising loss on real images and the mean-plus-covariance Gaussian clone coincide. Later, loss on real images becomes lower while the Gaussian clone stagnates. Figure 1 averages three network initializations and 5,000 test samples and shows generations gaining recognizable structure as training advances.

anchors.section: 2 A distributional simplicity bias in denoising diffusion models

key_findings.claim: The same clone-loss ordering appears on CelebA, but the replication is noisier and based on only two model initializations.
key_findings.evidence: CelebA is downscaled to 80 by 80 grayscale, and mean and mean-plus-covariance Gaussian clones are compared with real images. Figure 6 reports the same sequential separation over 100,000 examples, averaged across two U-Nets and 5,000 test samples; the authors attribute extra noise to the finite learning rate.

anchors.section: A.2 Sequential learning in CelebA data

key_findings.claim: The diffusion information exponent k* identifies the first statistical order jointly present in the data likelihood ratio and accessible through the denoising loss plus activation, and it controls online projected-SGD sample complexity in the single-spike model.
key_findings.evidence: k* is the smallest k for which the k-th Hermite coefficient of the likelihood ratio and the (k-1)-th coefficient of the effective nonlinearity are both nonzero. Propositions 4.3 and 4.4 give nearly matching success and failure thresholds of order d^(k*-1), with logarithmic factors and specified learning-rate conditions.

key_findings.claim: An isolated fourth-cumulant direction has k*=4 and requires more than cubic samples for the paper's online projected SGD to recover, even though other polynomial-time algorithms may need only quadratic samples.
key_findings.evidence: With no covariance spike and a Rademacher cumulant spike, weak recovery does not occur below the stated d^3 scale and does occur above the theorem threshold. The paper explicitly notes a d^(k*/2)=d^2 algorithmic detection lower scale and suggests smoothing could narrow the optimization-statistical gap, so d^3 is not an information-theoretic law for all learners.

key_findings.claim: When covariance and fourth-cumulant structure coexist, pairwise information is learned in quasi-linear samples while an independent cumulant remains cubic; positive correlation between their latent variables makes the cumulant recoverable in the same quasi-linear regime.
key_findings.evidence: Proposition 4.6 gives weak recovery of the covariance spike with Theta(d polylog d) samples. With independent latents the cumulant is not recovered below the cubic scale; with positively correlated latents and compatible initial signs, both spikes recover within the quasi-linear horizon. This formalizes a shortcut in which easy structure accelerates hard structure.

anchors.section: 4.2 Simplicity bias in denoising diffusion / Proposition 4.6

key_findings.claim: The spherical projection is not a harmless proof device in the one-neuron model: removing it can make common nonlinearities contract toward the trivial weight vector instead of learning the cumulant.
key_findings.evidence: The unprojected gradient contains an extra radial term. Proposition 4.7 shows that when its coefficient remains negative near the initialization, both the spike overlap and weight norm decay toward zero with high probability. Even the activation matched to the exact score satisfies this trapping condition in the paper's setting.

anchors.section: 4.4 The case of the optimal denoiser
B.7 Additional details for SGD without projection

key_findings.claim: Width and some forms of depth can overcome the one-neuron contraction, so the negative optimization result does not directly predict realistic network behavior.
key_findings.evidence: At dimension 100, a width-100 tied autoencoder trained with Adam or SGD recovers the cumulant direction while width one does not. Deeper tanh and sigmoid residual networks recover it, whereas deeper ReLU-squared networks lose recovery, plausibly from exploding activations. Results average five initializations and are activation- and optimizer-specific.

key_findings.claim: The theorem and the image experiment establish analogous orderings, not a quantitative explanation of U-Net learning times.
key_findings.evidence: The authors explicitly contrast Adam on richer architectures with online SGD on a single-neuron denoiser and state that an exact timescale match is not expected. Moreover, the image clone test only separates first/second moments from everything beyond them; it does not identify a fourth cumulant or measure the diffusion information exponent of CIFAR-10.

key_findings.claim: Despite being framed as a theory of generative diffusion, the main analysis does not characterize generated distributions or sampling quality.
key_findings.evidence: The setup states that it will not treat the generation process and instead focuses on learning the score. The empirical U-Net figures include qualitative generations, but the theorems concern spike recovery under a fixed-time denoising objective, not reverse-SDE error, sample diversity, fidelity, or memorization.

method.core_idea: Use moment-matched Gaussian clones to observe which distribution statistics a real denoiser exploits over training, then isolate covariance and non-Gaussian cumulant directions in a solvable spiked model and analyze their recovery through Hermite coefficients of the diffusion loss.
method.mechanism: The empirical half trains grayscale U-Nets with denoising score matching on CIFAR-10 and CelebA and evaluates the same model on Gaussian clones that match only the mean or both mean and covariance. The theoretical half uses a mixed cumulant model with a Gaussian variance spike u and a unit-variance non-Gaussian spike v, a rank-one nonlinear autoencoder with a skip connection, and online projected SGD. After applying Stein's lemma, the population-gradient expansion couples Hermite coefficients of the data likelihood ratio to an effective activation. Their first nonzero interaction defines k*, from which spike-recovery thresholds follow. The paper then removes projection to expose a radial attractor and runs finite-dimensional wider/deeper network experiments to test whether overparameterization escapes it.
assumptions: Equal denoising losses on real data and a moment-matched Gaussian clone imply that the network is not yet exploiting statistics absent from that clone.
Mean and covariance are appropriately called easy while all residual image structure is treated as higher-order complexity.
A distribution with one covariance spike and one fourth-cumulant spike captures the mechanism relevant to natural-image diffusion learning.
Online samples are independent, dimension tends to infinity, and the theorem's learning-rate, smoothness, sub-Gaussian, and sign conditions hold.
Weak recovery of a planted direction by one neuron's weight is a useful proxy for learning a distributional statistic.
Projected SGD on the unit sphere is a meaningful optimization protocol even though standard diffusion training does not impose that constraint.
Qualitative agreement between Adam-trained U-Nets and projected-SGD spike dynamics supports a common simplicity-bias mechanism despite different architectures and optimizers.
The fixed-noise denoising objective is informative about generative behavior even though reverse diffusion is not analyzed.

techniques.role: Compares real images with Gaussian datasets matching the mean or mean plus covariance to reveal when higher-order statistics affect loss.
Separates a pairwise covariance direction from a variance-matched non-Gaussian direction.
Expresses both the data likelihood ratio and effective denoising nonlinearity in an orthogonal basis.
Maps the first compatible pair of Hermite coefficients to projected-SGD sample complexity.
Keeps the one-neuron weight on the sphere and enables rigorous overlap dynamics.
Tests whether correlation between easy and hard planted variables accelerates higher-order recovery.
Shows how ordinary SGD can contract to a zero-weight solution after the spherical constraint is removed.
Uses wider tied autoencoders and residual networks to test whether realistic expressivity mitigates the trap.

evaluations.setting: Grayscale CIFAR-10 U-Net with 1,000 noise levels, Adam learning rate 1e-3, batch size 100
evaluations.metric: Test denoising loss on real, mean-only Gaussian, and mean-plus-covariance Gaussian datasets over training
evaluations.result: All losses initially coincide; real-data loss separates below the covariance clone after about 1,000 steps
evaluations.baseline: Moment-matched Gaussian clones; three network initializations and 5,000 test samples

evaluations.setting: 80 by 80 grayscale CelebA U-Net, Adam learning rate 1e-4
evaluations.metric: Clone and real-data denoising loss over training
evaluations.result: Qualitatively repeats the sequential ordering with noisier curves
evaluations.baseline: Mean-only and mean-plus-covariance clones; two initializations and 5,000 test examples

evaluations.setting: Single fourth-cumulant spike, rank-one denoiser, online projected SGD
evaluations.metric: Overlap with the planted direction as dimension and sample count scale
evaluations.result: k*=4 and recovery occurs on the cubic sample scale up to theorem logarithmic conditions
evaluations.baseline: Sub-cubic sample horizon and isotropic initialization

evaluations.metric: Weak recovery time for u and v
evaluations.result: Covariance is quasi-linear; the cumulant is cubic when latents are independent and quasi-linear when positively correlated
Several common and score-matched nonlinearities contract toward the zero solution under the theorem's sign condition
evaluations.baseline: Spherical projected SGD and rescaled nonlinearities

evaluations.setting: Dimension-100 mixed-cumulant data, tied autoencoders and feed-forward residual networks
evaluations.metric: Maximum normalized first-layer overlap with the planted cumulant direction
evaluations.result: Width 100 recovers where width one fails; depth helps tanh/sigmoid but hurts repeated ReLU-squared
evaluations.baseline: Widths, depths, activations, Adam versus SGD; five initializations

limitations: Reviewer-identified: the paper has no dedicated limitations section beyond caveats in its conclusion.
Reviewer-identified: the image experiments use grayscale CIFAR-10 and CelebA, only two or three seeds, and no confidence test for the claimed transition time.
Reviewer-identified: a mean-plus-covariance clone only shows that some non-Gaussian statistic matters; it cannot determine its cumulant order or identify a specific learned feature.
Reviewer-identified: the theoretical distribution has only one or two planted directions, unlike heterogeneous, local, and hierarchical natural-image statistics.

Reviewer-identified: the core theorem is for an online, one-neuron, fixed-noise denoiser with projected SGD, whereas the motivating experiment uses minibatch Adam and a U-Net across many noise levels.
Reviewer-identified: d^3 is an algorithm-specific projected-SGD scale, not an information-theoretic necessity; the paper itself notes a possible d^2 route for other algorithms.
Reviewer-identified: positive latent correlation produces a shortcut under sign-conditioned initialization, but its prevalence and sign structure in real data are not measured.
Reviewer-identified: the matched score activation becoming trapped under ordinary SGD is a property of the restricted parameterization, since width and depth can reverse it.
Reviewer-identified: finite-dimensional overparameterization experiments do not sweep dimension sufficiently to establish scaling laws for realistic networks.
Reviewer-identified: reverse-time sampling is explicitly excluded from the theory, so no result establishes sample fidelity, diversity, creativity, or memorization.
Reviewer-identified: qualitative samples in Figure 1 are not scored, and their relationship to clone-loss separation is not causally isolated.
Reviewer-identified: activation-specific failures and manual rescaling show that k* depends on the learner as well as the data, limiting any data-only complexity ranking.
failure_modes: A model can exploit a higher-order statistic that lowers denoising loss without improving reverse-sampling quality or semantic coherence.
Moment-matched clones can be out of distribution in obvious low-level ways, making loss separation easier than identifying natural higher-order structure.
Correlated easy features can hide a genuinely hard feature by carrying it through a shortcut; a curriculum inferred from marginal order alone will be wrong.
An activation whose Hermite spectrum misses the data's leading informative coefficient can exhibit a larger k* or never recover the feature.
Unprojected narrow models can collapse toward zero even when their functional form can represent the exact score.
Repeated squaring in deep ReLU-squared networks can explode activations and destroy the overlap despite greater depth.
A finite learning rate can blur or shift the empirical transition, as observed in CelebA.
Multiple interacting cumulants, multimodal manifolds, and local image features may not decompose into a single ordered sequence of pairwise then fourth-order learning.
The same test loss can conceal different generated distributions, so clone-loss curves alone can misdiagnose generative progress.
reusable_insights: Evaluate a learner throughout training on maximum-entropy clones that preserve selected statistics; divergence pinpoints when additional structure becomes behaviorally relevant.
Define difficulty jointly from the data distribution and the learner's accessible feature basis rather than assigning a fixed complexity to a statistic.
Correlate planted easy and hard factors to test whether a model learns the hard factor directly or rides an easy-feature shortcut.
Pair a positive sample-complexity theorem with a sub-threshold failure theorem so an apparent scaling law is not only sufficient.
Audit normalization constraints that look technical: projection can qualitatively change whether a feature is learnable.
Stress-test narrow-model optimization conclusions with width, depth, optimizer, and activation ablations before extrapolating to production networks.
Measure generated distributions in addition to denoising loss whenever the scientific claim concerns a generative model.
Track multiple statistical orders and noise levels jointly; a single scalar training step can hide different curricula across the diffusion schedule.
open_questions: Can a clone hierarchy matching third-, fourth-, local-patch, and multiscale statistics identify what real diffusion U-Nets learn at each phase?
What diffusion information exponent, if any, can be estimated for a convolutional U-Net on natural data rather than a planted one-neuron model?
Do clone-loss transition points predict improvements or regressions in FID, precision-recall, compositionality, and memorization?
How does k* change when the objective integrates the full diffusion-time distribution instead of fixing one noise level?
Can minibatch Adam dynamics be analyzed well enough to connect the theorem quantitatively to the observed thousand-step CIFAR transition?
Which natural-data correlations provide the quasi-linear shortcut for higher-order features, and do they improve robustness or merely encourage shortcuts?
Does width escape the zero attractor through neuron repulsion, feature diversity, skip-connection learning, or optimizer adaptivity?
Can activation or optimizer design reduce the projected-SGD cubic scale without prior knowledge of the relevant cumulant?
How do multiple non-Gaussian spikes compete, and does their learning order remain monotone in cumulant order?
What theory connects score-feature recovery to the complete reverse-SDE distribution and downstream sample quality?

competitive_landscape.title: Neural Networks Learn Statistics of Increasing Complexity
competitive_landscape.difference: Belrose et al. establish the distributional simplicity bias with maximum-entropy moment matching in classifiers and language models; this paper brings clone evaluation to image diffusion and derives an algorithm-specific exponent for covariance versus cumulant recovery.

competitive_landscape.title: An Analytical Theory of Spectral Bias in the Learning Dynamics of Diffusion Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Wang and Pehlevan solve full-batch learning and sampling for linear and convolutional denoisers and obtain inverse-variance ordering of covariance modes; this paper goes beyond second-order spectral structure to nonlinear higher-order cumulants and latent-correlation shortcuts, but does not solve sampling.

competitive_landscape.title: Understanding Generalizability of Diffusion Models Requires Rethinking the Hidden Gaussian Structure
competitive_landscape.difference: Li, Dai, and Qu observe that Gaussian mean-covariance structure is preferentially learned early and in the generalization regime; this paper explicitly measures departure from a covariance-matched clone and supplies a stylized sample-complexity theory for what comes next.

competitive_landscape.title: A solvable model of learning generative diffusion: theory and insights
competitive_landscape.difference: Cui, Pehlevan, and Lu analyze online-SGD training of a two-layer autoencoder and tightly characterize the generated distribution and mode collapse on Gaussian mixtures; this paper instead isolates higher-order feature recovery and optimizer traps, without characterizing generated samples.

competitive_landscape.title: Generalization Dynamics of Linear Diffusion Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Merger and Goldt derive training-test errors, sampling distributions, and an N approximately d memorization-generalization transition for linear denoisers; this paper studies nonlinear cumulant learning beyond Gaussian covariance but sacrifices direct sampling analysis.

competitive_landscape.title: Why Diffusion Models Don't Memorize: The Role of Implicit Dynamical Regularization in Training
competitive_landscape.difference: Bonnaire et al. separate early generation and later memorization times using U-Nets and a random-feature theory; this paper separates learning by statistical order and defines an exponent, not a generation-to-memorization window.

competitive_landscape.title: How compositional generalization and creativity improve as diffusion models are trained
competitive_landscape.difference: Favero et al. predict a hierarchy of context-dependent compositional features whose sample complexity grows with coherence scale and validate generated images and text; this paper orders covariance and cumulant features through Hermite interactions and correlated latents in a simpler spiked model.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Denoising diffusion models exhibit a distributional simplicity bias, and a diffusion information exponent determines when pairwise and higher-order statistics become learnable; correlated latent structure can collapse a cubic fourth-cumulant sample requirement to quasi-linear scale.
novelty_assessment.evidence: CIFAR-10 and CelebA Gaussian-clone experiments show early covariance-only behavior, while matching upper/lower projected-SGD results and a mixed-cumulant theorem establish separated and correlation-accelerated spike-recovery times in the stylized model.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The strongest novelty after prior Gaussian, spectral-bias, solvable-diffusion, and general distributional-simplicity work is the learner-dependent diffusion information exponent plus the formal covariance-to-cumulant shortcut under correlated latents. It is not yet a theory of realistic U-Net timescales or generated distributions; the empirical bridge establishes an analogy rather than validating the exponent on images.

reviewer_notes: Complete first-pass reading of all 22 cached pages, including theorem assumptions, proofs, architecture details, and negative results; seven competitors were checked against primary arXiv, OpenReview, or official NeurIPS records. Author claims and reviewer inference are separated. The central scope warning is explicit in the source: Adam-trained U-Nets and one-neuron online projected SGD agree qualitatively, but an exact timescale match is not expected, and reverse sampling is not analyzed. A second reviewer should check the theorem dependencies on the cited Ben Arous and Bardone-Goldt results before promotion to verified.
